## The question

The [channel-scaling study](../channel-scaling/index.qmd) measured the production channel DNS on
Snellius H100s: near-ideal weak scaling on one node, a drop to 47 % crossing to a second node. That
raised three questions this page answers:

1. **Is the inter-node drop "expected physics" or a defect?** A latency-bound global reduction
   costs ~log(nodes), so the expected weak-scaling shape is one visible drop at the node boundary,
   then a near-plateau. One multi-node data point cannot distinguish that from continued decay —
   here we extend to 32 GPUs (8 nodes) and *decompose the time per step* into predictor / momentum
   solve / pressure projection / global reductions, with the pressure iteration count separated
   from the per-iteration cost.
2. **How does the CPU path scale?** Weak scaling under MPI × OpenMP hybrid parallelism, from a
   24-core workstation to Snellius Genoa nodes (192 cores each).
3. **How does `peclet.flow` compare to the field?** The same case, run by
   [CaNS](https://github.com/CaNS-World/CaNS) (the methodologically closest state-of-the-art
   solver: 2nd-order staggered FD, FFT-based direct Poisson solve, published scaling to tens of
   thousands of cores) and by **OpenFOAM** (the most widely used open-source CFD code).

## The instrument: a boundary-free Taylor–Green box

Scaling studies want a case that grows without complications. We tile a triply periodic box with
**Taylor–Green vortices** (one vortex per $64^3$ tile, $\mathrm{Re}_\text{tile}=100$): no walls, no
immersed geometry, every cell does identical work, and the domain extends in any direction by adding
tiles. The TGV initial condition is also a Stokes eigenfunction, which gives the driver a built-in
analytic correctness check (backward-Euler decay factor matched to $2\times10^{-3}$, identical
across rank counts).

[`tgv_bench.py`](tgv_bench.py) runs the case distributed (core ORB decomposition) and reports
warmup-excluded per-step wall time with the solver's new per-phase instrumentation:

- **predictor** (ghost fills, RHS/advection builds), **momentum** (implicit diffusion solves),
  **projection** (cut-cell pressure multigrid) — device-fenced phase times per rank;
- **pressure iterations per step** — so algorithmic drift (more Krylov iterations on a bigger
  global problem) is never conflated with communication cost;
- **global-reduction tax** — accumulated wall time and count of every `MPI_Allreduce` inside the
  pressure solve, the latency-bound term of distributed incompressible CFD.

## Workstation baseline (Threadripper PRO 5965WX, RTX 5080)

Before the supercomputer: everything measurable on one machine — a 24-core Threadripper PRO 5965WX
(8-channel DDR4) with an RTX 5080 (16 GB). Three questions: what is the best MPI × OpenMP mix on one
node, how do the three codes weak-scale within a node, and where does a consumer GPU land.

### The instrument found (and fixed) a real decomposition bug

The very first sweep produced the study's first result. At **non-power-of-two rank counts** the ORB
decomposition was badly imbalanced (blocks from 86 k to 1.05 M cells at np = 24 on $192^3$) *and*
the pressure multigrid lost its coarse levels — **27 pressure iterations/step instead of 8**, and
114 on the weak-scaling grid. Root cause: the decomposition was aligned to the grid's *natural
maximum* coarsening depth (align 64 for $192^3$, 1024 for a 3072-cell axis), which over-constrains
the ORB — the aligned split snap turns a balanced 96|96 into 128|64, and sub-boxes below twice the
alignment skip alignment entirely, collapsing the multigrid's even-coarsening gate. Capping the
alignment at $2^4$ (all the default 5-level hierarchy needs) fixes both at once:

![Before/after the `coarsenAlignment` cap. Bars: ms/step (log); annotations: pressure
iterations/step. Every parallel configuration improves; the broken cases recover
5–6×.](workstation_alignfix.png)

The fix is validated bit-exact where it should be (33/33 flow MPI ctests) and shipped in `flow`.
At power-of-two rank counts nothing changes — which is why the channel-scaling study (np = 1…8)
never saw it. *A lesson for the decomposition-anatomy section below: rank counts off the
power-of-two grid exercise entirely different ORB paths.*

### The first comparison run made the solver 2.9× faster on CPU (and 1.5× on GPU)

The first head-to-head was humbling: serial peclet ran at 0.35 Mcell/s — *slower than OpenFOAM*
(0.47). The per-phase instrumentation decomposed the gap into three findings, each fixed and
measured in `flow`:

1. **A fixed momentum sweep count from a stiffer regime.** The benchmark inherited 20 Red–Black
   Gauss–Seidel sweeps per velocity component — sized for large-d$t$/porous production runs. At
   this case's diffusion number (~0.13) five sweeps fully converge (ablation: 20→5 sweeps changes
   the analytic-decay check by nothing and saves a third of the step). The structural fix is a
   **tolerance-based stop** (`set_velocity_solver_params(iters, rtol)`): the sweep loop ends once
   the max velocity increment has contracted to `rtol` of the first sweep's, with the check fused
   into the sweep kernel. Easy regimes exit at 3–5 sweeps; stiff regimes still run to the cap.
2. **Kokkos' default host MDRange tiling was a hidden 2–5× tax.** Rewriting the RB-GS smoothers in
   a host-only line-sweep form (one $(y,z)$ pencil per task, contiguous stride-2 $x$-loop —
   bit-identical, since same-colour cells are independent) gave **5.6× on the momentum sweep** and
   1.7× on the projection; the same full-$x$-row tiling applied to the elementwise and reduction
   kernels added more. The device code path is untouched by construction (compile-time selection),
   verified: with legacy settings the GPU reproduces its baseline **to the decimal**.
3. **The pressure solve issued ~17.6 global all-reduces per Krylov iteration** — dot products,
   residual maxima, and a nullspace (mean) projection at *every multigrid level* costing two
   all-reduces each. Fusing the mean-removal's {sum, count} pair into one `MPI_Allreduce`
   (bit-identical) and dropping the interior-level projections (`set_pressure_mean_removal("fine")`
   — the operator preserves mean-freeness, so the Krylov iteration never sees the dropped
   components) brings it to **5.4 per iteration, with iteration counts exactly unchanged**. On one
   node this is invisible; across nodes each all-reduce is a latency hit, so this ~3× matters
   exactly where the channel study saw the inter-node drop. The Chebyshev driver inherits the same
   diet through the shared V-cycle (13 → ~3 per iteration).

Net effect, all correctness gates green (33/33 MPI ctests, GPU regression suite at +0.00 %,
analytic checks digit-identical): **serial CPU 5969 → 2047 ms/step (2.9×), single GPU 155.7 →
105.3 ms/step (1.48×)**. Every number below is the improved solver.

### Hybrid mix: some MPI is good, all-MPI is not

![Left: throughput by MPI ranks × OpenMP threads on 24 cores (fixed $192^3$ TGV). Right: the
per-phase step decomposition.](workstation_mix.png)

**12 ranks × 2 threads is the sweet spot (11.8 Mcell/s)** — vs 9.8 for pure MPI (24×1) and a
14× speedup over serial. The phase split shows why: the momentum solve and the pressure projection
are memory-bandwidth-bound sweeps, so what matters is keeping all memory channels fed without
paying 24 ranks' worth of halo surface and per-rank multigrid boilerplate. The global-reduction
term is invisible on one node (< 2 ms/step) — it only matters across nodes.

### Weak scaling within one node: bandwidth is the wall, and peclet now holds the best curve

![Weak scaling at 2.1 M cells/rank (grid $128n\times128\times128$), pure MPI, up to 24 cores.
Left: efficiency vs. own 1-rank baseline. Right: absolute throughput (log scale); the dotted line
is the single RTX 5080 running the same case.](workstation_weak.png)

With per-rank work fixed, all four codes decay together — **and this is not communication**:
peclet's pressure iteration count stays at exactly 7.0 per step at every rank count. A single
node's weak scaling measures **shared memory-bandwidth saturation**, nothing else — the efficiency
ordering (incflo 43 %, peclet 40 %, CaNS 31 %, OpenFOAM 29 % at 24 ranks) is simply the *inverse*
of per-core bandwidth demand: the slower a code streams per core-second, the later the shared
memory system saturates. Absolute CPU throughput on 24 cores: **CaNS 41 Mcell/s, peclet 9.8,
incflo 4.4, OpenFOAM 3.3**. Three comparisons worth separating:

- **vs OpenFOAM** (the ubiquitous general-purpose reference): peclet is **3× faster** at identical
  settings.
- **vs incflo** (the AMReX exascale solver in peclet's *own method family* — finite-volume
  incompressible NS, geometric-multigrid projections, embedded-boundary capable): peclet is
  **2.2× faster on CPU** (2.4× per core) — winning its own game against the state of the art that
  shares its design constraints. *Fairness note: incflo runs here with expert-tuned settings, not
  defaults — we measured the ablation (`max_grid_size` 32→64: 1.25×; MLMG tolerances matched to
  the study's 1e-5 instead of AMReX's ~1e-11 default: 1.31×; combined 1.53×) and report the tuned
  numbers.*
- **vs CaNS** (the FFT ceiling): the remaining 4× is the price of generality stated honestly — an
  explicit RK3 step plus an exact FFT solve that exists *only because* the box is trivial, against
  an implicit step and a geometric multigrid that handle arbitrary cut-cell geometry at large
  d$t$.

**And the single RTX 5080 at 67 Mcell/s outruns CaNS's entire 24-core node by 1.6×** running the
identical case — the design point of the suite: the CPU path is a capable oracle, the GPU path is
the product.

### Single-GPU ladder (RTX 5080, 16 GB)

| grid | cells | ms/step | Mcell/s | pressure iters |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| $128^3$ | 2.1 M | 31.1 | 67.4 | 7.0 |
| $160^3$ | 4.1 M | 67.5 | 60.7 | 9.5 |
| $192^3$ | 7.1 M | 105.3 | 67.2 | 8.9 |
| $208^3$ | 9.0 M | 265.0 | 34.0 | 19.6 |

Steady ~60–67 Mcell/s until 16 GB fills. The $208^3$ outlier is *algorithmic*, not hardware: 208
supports only a $13^3$-bottomed multigrid whose odd coarse level weakens the preconditioner
(19.6 iterations). Grids with generous power-of-two content keep the hierarchy deep — the same
divisibility theme as the decomposition story.

## Cross-node CPU weak scaling on Snellius Genoa: the structural argument, measured

The head-to-head the study was built for: 188.7 M cells *per node* (768×640×384 each), grown with
the node count on Snellius Genoa (192 cores/node), every code on the identical tiled-TGV case.
peclet runs its measured single-node optimum (96 ranks × 2 threads, which alone delivers
59 Mcell/s — 6× the whole 24-core workstation); the references run their natural pure-MPI mode.

**Methodology note that is itself a finding:** single scaling measurements on a busy cluster are
noise. The same peclet configuration measured 3.2 s and 8.0 s per step on different node
allocations before we pinned cores (`--cpu-bind=cores`) and took three draws per point. Bound
draws reproduce to ±5 %; the figure shows every draw (open markers) and the median (line). CaNS
and incflo points are single draws — their *large* features are far outside this noise band, but
their small wiggles are not interpretable.

![Cross-node weak scaling on Snellius Genoa, 188.7 Mcells/node fixed. Left: efficiency vs own
1-node baseline (open circles: individual peclet draws). Right: aggregate throughput; the dotted
line is ideal scaling at peclet's slope.](snellius_weak.png)

| nodes | peclet (median) | CaNS | incflo |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 45 Mcell/s — 100 % | **109 — 100 %** | 16 — 100 % |
| 2 | 86 — 96 % | 20 — 9 % | 21 — 67 % |
| 4 | 167 — 93 % | 153 — 35 % | 49 — 77 % |
| 8 | **266 — 74 %** | 45 — **5 %** | — |

Three structural results:

1. **peclet holds the flattest curve in the field** — 96/93/74 % at 2/4/8 nodes, iterations
   pinned at 8.1 throughout, and the measured all-reduce cost growing like the expected
   latency-bound log-term (153 → 431 ms/step, ~9 % of the step at 8 nodes). This is the "one-time
   inter-node cost, then a gentle slope" shape the study set out to verify.
2. **CaNS's single-node crown does not survive the interconnect.** 2.4× faster than peclet on one
   node — and by two nodes it has collapsed to 9 % efficiency (reproduced in independent runs),
   at eight nodes to 5 %: **eight CaNS nodes deliver the throughput of one peclet node.** The FFT
   direct solve's global all-to-all transposes are cheap in shared memory and ruinous across
   nodes; peclet's halo + reduction structure is precisely what avoids this. (Caveat stated
   honestly: CaNS ran with its automatic pencil-grid choice; expert `dims` tuning may soften —
   but cannot remove — the all-to-all tax.)
3. **Against its own method family, peclet wins on both axes**: ~3× incflo per node *and* the
   flatter curve (93 % vs 77 % at 4 nodes).

The crossover happens **before two nodes**: any problem too big for a single node is already a
problem where peclet outruns the FFT state of the art. *(OpenFOAM's cross-node points — same ESI
v2412 built from source on Snellius — are compiling and will complete this figure.)*

## Decomposition anatomy: is a prime rank count much worse than a power of two?

**After the alignment fix: no.** Sweeping awkward rank counts on the fixed $192^3$ box
(pure MPI, 5965WX, final solver):

| ranks | ms/step | Mcell/s | pressure iters | max-block imbalance |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 5 | 2634 | 2.7 | 8.0 | 1.04× |
| 7 (prime) | 2015 | 3.5 | 8.0 | 1.02× |
| **8** | 1579 | 4.5 | **6.9** | 1.00× |
| 13 (prime) | 1186 | 6.0 | 7.9 | 1.08× |
| **16** | 945 | 7.5 | **7.2** | 1.00× |
| 23 (prime) | 819 | 8.6 | 8.0 | 1.20× |

Non-power-of-two counts pay exactly **one extra pressure iteration** (the ORB's uneven-subtree
splits land off the deepest coarsening grid, so the multigrid loses its bottom level) and a ≤ 20 %
max-block imbalance at the worst prime — both minor; throughput sits on the same trend line as the
neighbouring powers of two. *Before* the fix the same experiment produced 27–114 iterations/step
and up to 12:1 imbalance — the difference between "prime rank counts are mildly suboptimal" and
"prime rank counts are catastrophic" was a bug, not a law of nature. Multi-node topology effects
(slab vs pencil vs brick at scale) are measured in the Snellius sections above.
